name: Wagner's Generalized Birthday Problem / k-Tree and Modular Linear Algebra over Z_m
description: Wagner's generalized birthday problem (GBP) asks, given k lists of n-bit values, for one element from each list whose sum (XOR in (Z_2)^n, or addition mod m) is zero. Wagner's k-tree algorithm solves it by repeatedly merging pairs of lists and filtering on prescribed low-order bits, keeping list sizes balanced; heuristically it runs in time and memory O(k * 2^{n/(1+log k)}) (for k a power of two), so k=4 gives O(2^{n/3}) and larger k drives the exponent down. The modular version solves constrained subset-sum-like equations over Z_m (Random Modular Subset Sum, multi-set dense subset sum) and is the source of 2^{n/log n}-style subexponential bounds for dense instances: Lyubashevsky (2005) proves a modified k-tree solves Random Modular Subset Sum with modulus M = 2^{n^eps} (eps<1) in time and space 2^{O(n^eps / log n)} = M^{O(1/log n)}, and Shallue (ANTS 2008) refines this for asymptotic density below n/(log n)^2. The technique has become a standard cryptanalytic tool for knapsack, SIS, hash collisions and Equihash. Crucially, these are average-case / many-solution results and do not break the O*(2^{n/2}) worst-case barrier for Subset Sum.
worst_case_time: k-tree (Wagner, CRYPTO 2002): for k = 2^d lists of n-bit values, time (and memory) O(k * 2^{n/(d+1)}) under the heuristic list-size assumption; equivalently O(k * M^{1/(1+log k)}) group operations for modulus M = 2^n. For k = 4 this is O(2^{n/3}); for k = 2 lists it recovers the classical birthday O(2^{n/2}). Lyubashevsky's provable variant (2005): Random Modular Subset Sum with M = 2^{n^eps}, eps<1, in time 2^{O(n^eps/log n)} = M^{O(1/log n)} with success probability 1 - 2^{-Omega(n^eps)}. Shallue (ANTS 2008): fastest known for asymptotic density below n/(log n)^2, again 2^{O(n^eps/log n)}. All are average-case over random inputs, not worst-case.
space_complexity: k-tree uses memory of the same order as its running time, O(k * 2^{n/(d+1)}); reducing memory is Wagner's first open problem. Tradeoffs (Nikolic-Sasaki, Biryukov-Khovratovich, Dinur 2018) give curves such as T^2 M^{floor(log K)-1} = N and T^{ceil((log K)/2)+1} M^{floor((log K)/2)} = N. Dinur improves small K: K=6 with T=N^{1/3}, M=N^{1/6}; K=14 with T=N^{1/4}, M=N^{1/8}. Lyubashevsky's algorithm uses 2^{O(n^eps/log n)} time and space.
model: Classical random-access machine / word RAM with sorting, merging and group operations (XOR over (Z_2)^n, or addition in Z_m). The rigorous analyses model the input as independent uniform random values; the k-tree success is a high-probability average-case statement. Some cryptographic applications use a random function H (random-oracle heuristic).
randomized_or_deterministic: Randomized (Monte Carlo): succeeds with high probability on random instances. Wagner's original analysis is heuristic; rigorous high-probability analyses were given by Lyubashevsky (2005), Shallue (2008), Minder-Sinclair (SODA 2009) and Lin-Vasudevan (2024). It is not deterministic and not worst-case.
time_space_tradeoff_curve: A full family parameterized by the number of lists k (K in Dinur's notation) and the memory M. Wagner's k-tree sits at T = M = N^{1/(floor(log K)+1)} (N = 2^n). Dinur (2018) improves the curve to T^{ceil((log K)/2)+1} M^{floor((log K)/2)} = N for K >= 8 and to T^2 M^{floor(log K)-1} = N, e.g. K=8: T^3 M = N (from the previous T^2 M^2 = N), K=32: T^4 M^2 = N. For non-powers of two, K in {6,7,14,15} match the k-tree time with much less memory. For k=4 the single point is T = M = N^{1/3}.
numerical_exponent_and_record_year: k=4: O(2^{n/3}) (Wagner, CRYPTO 2002) - the source of 2^{n/3} for 4-list problems. Lyubashevsky (2005): 2^{O(n^eps/log n)} for M = 2^{n^eps}, giving a 2^{O(n/log n)}-style bound for dense modular subset sum. Shallue (ANTS 2008): multi-set improvement for density < n/(log n)^2. Dinur (2018): K=6 -> T=N^{1/3}, M=N^{1/6}; K=14 -> T=N^{1/4}, M=N^{1/8}.
problem_variant: Generalized birthday problem / k-SUM / k-XOR (one element from each of k lists summing to zero); Random Modular Subset Sum (RMSS); multi-set / dense subset sum; and constrained subset-sum-like linear equations over Z_m. Also used for SIS, low-weight knapsack, subset/product problems, and hash-collision (Equihash).
applies_to: Random high-density modular subset sum with modulus M = 2^{n^eps}, eps<1 (Lyubashevsky); dense / multi-set subset sum of asymptotic density below n/(log n)^2 (Shallue); the k-list GBP over (Z_2)^n or Z_m for arbitrary k (Wagner, Minder-Sinclair, Dinur); cryptanalytic instances where the solution set is large (many representations). It does not solve unique-solution worst-case Subset Sum.
coefficient_set: The underlying selection is binary: each list contributes at most one chosen element, so the equation sum_i x_i a_i = t (mod m) has x_i in {0,1} with exactly k chosen terms in the k-list formulation. This is a 0/1 coefficient set with a fixed-cardinality (k-selection) structure. For multi-set dense subset sum, coefficients are bounded multiplicities.
density_regime: High / medium density. RMSS density is d = n/log2(M); Lyubashevsky targets M = 2^{n^eps}, i.e. high density with many solutions, and assumes n^eps = omega(log n). Shallue's variant targets asymptotic density below n/(log n)^2. The method presupposes that the expected number of solutions is at least one (pigeonhole), so it is fundamentally a high-density / many-solution technique.
solution_regime: Promised / numerous-solution regime. The birthday filter only helps when solutions are abundant; it finds one of many rather than certifying a unique solution, and it gives no worst-case guarantee.
cardinality_constraint: Yes at the structural level: the k-list GBP fixes that exactly one element is chosen from each of the k lists, i.e. a fixed-cardinality (Hamming-weight-k) selection over the list positions. This structure is what makes the pairwise merge and modular filtering work.
key_technique: Wagner's k-tree / generalized birthday algorithm: partition the input into k lists, then build a balanced binary merge tree; at each internal node merge two child lists and keep only pairs whose value matches a prescribed set of low-order bits (or coordinates) modulo the modulus. The list-merging (birthday) lemma keeps the expected list sizes geometrically balanced so that lists of size about M^{1/(1+log k)} suffice, and the final merge yields the global zero. The modular variant performs the merges with modular addition and filters on residue classes, effectively solving a constrained linear/subset-sum equation over Z_m.
core_idea: Filtering each merge on a fraction of the n bit positions forces the number of surviving pairs to shrink by a controlled factor. Starting from k lists of size M^{1/(1+log k)}, the expected count of partial collisions at each level stays constant, so the birthday effect guarantees many partial matches and a final solution. Because the filtering is over modular residues, this is a combinatorial way to solve linear equations over Z_m without Gaussian elimination on an exponentially large solution space, and increasing k lowers the exponent toward n/log n.
reduction_pipeline: Dense / Random Modular Subset Sum -> split the n items into k groups -> constrained k-sum / generalized birthday over Z_m -> Wagner k-tree pairwise modular filtering -> witness. Multi-set dense subset sum -> multi-set birthday (Shallue). Knapsack / SIS / low-weight syndrome decoding -> modular linear equation -> GBP (with representation techniques for low density).
constructive_vs_existential: Constructive: the algorithm outputs the explicit list of k elements (a witness array of indices), not merely a proof of existence.
search_vs_decision_witness: It is a search algorithm: it returns an explicit witness (the chosen elements) with high probability, rather than deciding feasibility.
obstacle_to_2n3: The method relies on there being many solutions (high density / pigeonhole). For unique-solution or low-density worst-case Subset Sum, the number of candidates is too small for the birthday filter to make progress, and the lists remain large, so the algorithm degenerates to (or is worse than) 2^{n/2} meet-in-the-middle; no worst-case 2^{n/3} bound follows. Even at k=4, reaching 2^{n/3} would require solving a hard 4-list instance, and the k-tree's success at that size needs balanced lists of length ~2^{n/3} plus rigorous slack, which is not available in the unique-solution regime. Thus the 2^{n/log n} bounds apply only to dense/random instances, not to the worst-case problem where the MITM barrier (and the 2^{n/3} question) lives.
potential_to_break_mitm: medium for average-case / random high-density instances (it genuinely beats 2^{n/2} there, giving 2^{n/log n}-style bounds); low for worst-case Subset Sum, which is the setting of the 2^{n/3} question.
barrier_evidence: The k-tree is an average-case algorithm; the k-SUM conjecture and SETH-based lower bounds constrain worst-case improvements. Wagner's heuristic analysis was shown by Lyubashevsky, Shallue, Minder-Sinclair and Lin-Vasudevan to require strictly larger lists for high success probability, so the heuristic exponent understates the rigorous cost. Dinur-Keller-Klein and related work give lower bounds showing the k=3,4,5 list-algorithm complexities are optimal in certain density regimes. No worst-case reduction from Subset Sum to dense GBP is known.
open_questions: Wagner's two stated open problems: (1) efficient time-memory tradeoffs for GBP (progress by Nikolic-Sasaki, Biryukov-Khovratovich, Dinur 2018; still open in general); (2) complexity for K not a power of two (progress for K in {6,7,14,15} by Dinur). Further: can the average-case 2^{n/log n} bounds be extended to worst-case or unique-solution instances? Can the modular variant be derandomized? Can the rigorous list-size slack be eliminated (Lin-Vasudevan 2024 give asymptotically tight bounds for a wide range)?
conditional_hypothesis: The positive average-case results assume uniformly random instances (and a random function H in cryptographic applications, i.e. a random-oracle heuristic); there is no lattice assumption. The surrounding worst-case hardness context uses the k-SUM conjecture and SETH.
worst_case_vs_average_case_guarantee: Average-case only. Guarantees hold for random modular subset sum / random dense instances with high probability; no worst-case guarantee is claimed.
cryptographic_regime: Directly cryptanalytic. Wagner motivated GBP by a subexponential attack on Schnorr and Okamoto-Schnorr blind signatures over elliptic curves (suggesting 1600-bit moduli). The k-tree underpins attacks on knapsack encryption, low-weight / inhomogeneous SIS (which formalizes collision finding), code-based schemes (Wave, CROSS, LESS), hash-based designs, and Equihash/Zcash proof-of-work. Density: high-density RMSS (d<1); for low-density knapsack, generalized-birthday/representation methods (Howgrave-Graham-Joux, Becker-Coron-Joux) give 2^{0.29n}-style results rather than the dense 2^{n/log n}.
pseudopolynomial_interaction: Complements DP / pseudopolynomial methods: for small moduli M = 2^{O(log^2 n)} polynomial-time algorithms exist (Flaxman-Przydatek, STACS 2005; Lyubashevsky generalizes to M = 2^{c log^2 n}) and ordinary DP solves M = poly(n). The generalized birthday fills the medium/high-density gap between DP and lattice / meet-in-the-middle methods, and multi-set variants handle bounded multiplicities.

empirical_evidence: Wagner's paper reports concrete parameter choices and a subexponential attack on Schnorr/Okamoto-Schnorr blind signatures with suggested 1600-bit moduli. FSBday (Bernstein, Lange, et al.) implements and benchmarks Wagner's attack on the FSB hash-based compression/signature proposal. Lin-Vasudevan (2024) present experimental evaluation of the tightness of their k-tree success/complexity bounds.
implementation_artifact: FSBday implements Wagner's generalized birthday attack (https://cryptojedi.org/papers/fsbday-20090617.pdf); Wagner-style merges also appear in Equihash/Zcash mining code. [uncertain] whether an official reference implementation of Lyubashevsky's provable variant or Shallue's multi-set algorithm is publicly available.
verification_method: Re-derive the list-merging lemma (balance of expected list sizes after filtering on a fraction of coordinates) and the k-tree success probability; check that the chosen k and list size reproduce the claimed exponent M^{1/(1+log k)} or 2^{O(n^eps/log n)}. Reproduce FSBday on the published parameters. Run the efficient bound-computation algorithm of Lin-Vasudevan for concrete (k, list size, modulus) settings and compare with experiments.
